title: Barack Obama on the Trump Administration’s Intimidation Campaign Against Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
content:
Barack Obama, in a 430-word essay:

It is a basic principle of American democracy that the government can’t selectively target individuals simply because of their political beliefs or what they say. But that’s exactly what the Trump Administration is doing to Congresswoman Ilhan Omar of Minnesota. [...]

The fact that any president, or any administration, is willing to engage in such transparent efforts to intimidate someone should outrage all Americans, regardless of how they feel about Congresswoman Omar’s political views. Because if this becomes the new normal, there’s no reason to believe it will stop with her — or that future presidents, in either party, won’t do the same.

Thoughtful, sharp, and eloquent as ever.

But Obama posted this essay on X, which, I have been told in the past week, shows that he in fact is a Nazi sympathizer, a fascist, a pedophile, and unconcerned about racism. As surprised as I was to learn those things about myself, I’m equally surprised to learn them about President Obama, whom I heretofore considered a thoughtful statesman and moral compass.

Either that, or, Threads, Bluesky, and Mastodon have relegated themselves into irrelevance by allowing their discourse to be dominated by a fringe of unhinged kooks who want to be angry and want everyone else to be angry.

 ★

title: Book Review: Quackery - A Brief History of the Worst Ways to Cure Everything by Lydia Kang ★★★⯪☆
content:
This is a charming and funny book all about the various ways humans have promoted fake medical cures in exchange for money.

Despite the grim (and occasionally distressing) subject matter, the tone remains light and poppy throughout. There are lots of snarky asides (especially about the fake medical practitioners) and a real appreciation for the bizarre. It's fun the whole way through, although sometimes at the expense of people who perhaps didn't know better than to trust charlatans.

One thing that is constantly brought back is how it can be hard to determine what is patent nonsense and what is a bone fide cure:

Prevent blood clotting: Extract mucus from the intestinal membranes of slaughtered pigs or from the lungs of slaughtered cows. Inject. (heparin)

Is that any more believable than injecting goat testicles to cure impotence?

It also brings to light how squeamish we can be, especially when faced with unusual medical procedures:

We borrow other people’s wombs for surrogacy. And yet, plenty of people squirm at the idea of breastmilk banks. We are a society of contradictions.

The eBook is beautifully formatted. For once, images are in-line with the text! Usually in books of this sort, publishers treat the eBook like a mass-market paperback and stick the illustrations at the end.

It ends rather abruptly, after taking us through light, electricity, colour therapy, animal magnetism, and a couple of dozen other "cure-alls"

Sadly, there are no references or footnotes. While I have no reason to doubt the veracity of the claims, for a book about scientific misinformation and malpractice, I'd've expected a way to find out more information.

title: Why do we need ud2 when int 6 is right there?
content:
Some time ago, I mentioned that the ud2 instruction was created to be an architecturally undefined instruction. But why not just use an int 6 instruction? It’s a two-byte instruction, just like ud2, and interrupt vector 6 is the invalid opcode vector, so a program could just invoke it manually and get whatever behavior the operating system assigns to an attempt to execute an invalid opcode.

Well, not exactly.

Architecturally, the invalid opcode is a fault, which means that the address of the faulting instruction is reported to the exception handler. On the other hand, the int 6 is a trap, which means that the address of the instruction after the int 6 is reported to the handler.

This distinction between faults and traps reflects how they are used. A fault represents an error that the kernel could attempt to repair and retry. For example, a page fault could be repaired by paging the memory in. An access violation could be repaired by changing the page protections. A trap reports an operation that has already occurred and gives you a chance to do some special work in response to it before resuming execution. In the case of a software interrupt, the handler wants to process whatever the interrupt means, and then resume execution with the next instruction.

Now, some faults are unlikely to be repaired, but reporting them as faults means that you have to take extra steps if you want to execute past them. If you just ignore the fault, the instruction restarts and faults again.

If you manually raise the int 6 interrupt to simulate a #UD undefined instruction fault, the handler will think it’s dealing with a CPU-generated undefined instruction fault, so it expects the instruction pointer in the fault frame to point to the undefined instruction. But since int puts the address of the next instruction into the fault frame, the fault handler will look at the instruction and get confused as to why the invalid instruction fault was raised. “It says here that the faulting instruction is a xor eax, eax. That’s a perfectly legitimate instruction. Why did it fault?”

One case for inspecting the faulting instruction is to emulate missing instructions on older processors.

Furthermore, in protected mode, you need to have permission to issue an int 6. The interrupt descriptor table describes what to do for each interrupt, as well as what CPU privilege level is permitted to invoke it explicitly. And to avoid exactly these types of problems where a user-mode program issues an int 6 and confuses the #UD handler, all operating systems deny int 6 privileges to user mode.

So even if you try to fake a #UD via an explicit int 6, it doesn’t work. To get the #UD undefined instruction fault, you have to issue an actual undefined instruction.

The post Why do we need <CODE>ud2</CODE> when <CODE>int 6</CODE> is right there? appeared first on The Old New Thing.

title: NixOS Is Making Me Less Afraid
content:
Something funny happened a little while ago: I read about FreshRSS, and it sounded nice, so I installed it on a server and started using it. That would not have happened a year ago, but then again, a year ago I didn’t have any NixOS servers.

For the past few years, my RSS feeds have lived locally on my phone only. There was a good idea behind that, but it never quite worked in practice. For one, many things are easier to read on a larger screen. But it was also brittle to trust a phone app to manage the read/unread status of thousands of articles across a hundred feeds. What I really wanted was a server-side feed aggregator. This is software that runs on a server, manages RSS feeds, and then I can read the RSS feeds either through a web interface, or through client applications. I’ve wanted that for a while, but I’ve never taken the step, because it would be yet another side project to maintain the deployment of.

But now, with some NixOS experience, adding a working FreshRSS configuration (including backups) took 9 lines of Nix code. That installation has just hands-off worked for the past few months. If or when that server breaks, I can spin up a new one running the exact same configuration, probably in something like 15 minutes. When we can do something like that, there is literally no reason to not just try the new software.

title: No More Icons In Every Menu By Default
content:
Have you heard the good news? I bemoaned the approach of putting an icon in every menu item by default which shipped with macOS Tahoe — but now it’s gone in Golden Gate!

John Gruber wrote about this reversion back in June, including the fact that Apple’s new Human Interface Guidelines specifically call out Tahoe’s approach to menus as an example of what not to do on macOS.

As the old saying goes, it takes a big man corporation to admit when they’re wrong.

As I mentioned in my original post, one of the arguments I had in my quiver against this practice was “Apple doesn’t do it”. But once Apple started putting icons in all their menus in Tahoe, I lost a persuasive point in my argument.

But now, I think I have an argument that’s even stronger than before!

It’s no longer: “Apple doesn’t put icons in their menus.”

It’s: “Apple tried putting icons in all their menus, and even they went back on it!”

They designed it, shipped it, lived with it for a year, then publicly changed their guidance on it. To me, that’s a lot more persuasive than simply saying, “Apple doesn’t do this.”

Choosing not to do something you’ve never done is one thing.

Choosing not to do something you’ve done is experience.

That’s the essence of life: learning by doing.
